title: The Timestomper
subtitle: File System Forensics — MAC Time Manipulation
narrative: A corporate whistleblower claims that a disgruntled sysadmin deleted critical HR documents before resigning. The sysadmin's workstation has been imaged. Your job: find the tampered files and prove the timestamps were falsified.
learningObjective: Understand how timestomping works by comparing $STANDARD_INFORMATION vs $FILE_NAME attributes in the NTFS Master File Table (MFT). Recognize that anti-forensic tools modify SI timestamps but often leave FN timestamps untouched.

preQuiz.question: In NTFS, which metadata attribute stores the timestamps visible in Windows Explorer?
preQuiz.explanation: $STANDARD_INFORMATION stores the timestamps shown in Windows Explorer and most forensic tools by default. This is also the attribute most commonly targeted by timestomping tools.

preQuiz.question: What is 'timestomping'?
options: Modifying MAC times to hide when a file was really created or accessed
Deleting the MFT entry for a file
Compressing timestamps to save disk space
preQuiz.explanation: Timestomping is the deliberate modification of a file's MAC (Modified, Accessed, Created) timestamps to mislead investigators about the true timeline of events.

hints.text: In NTFS, every file has two timestamp records. Most tools only show you one. Try comparing them.
Look at the Documents folder. Notice anything unusual about when the files were supposedly last modified?
When all four MAC timestamps of a file are identical down to the second, that is almost always the fingerprint of a timestomping tool. Now find the tool itself.

debriefing.title: How Timestomping Works
debriefing.concept: NTFS stores two independent sets of timestamps per file: $STANDARD_INFORMATION ($SI) and $FILE_NAME ($FN). Timestomping tools like Timestomp.exe or Metasploit's timestamp module only modify the $SI attribute — because that is what Windows APIs expose. The $FN attribute, updated directly by the NTFS kernel driver, is much harder to forge and often retains the true timestamps. A mismatch between $SI and $FN is a red flag.
debriefing.realWorldTool: Tools like Autopsy, FTK Imager, and the Sleuth Kit's 'istat' command can display both $SI and $FN timestamps simultaneously. Analysts specifically look for this discrepancy.
debriefing.caseConnection: In this case, the $SI timestamps were all set to the exact same second — a telltale sign. The $FN timestamps, combined with the Security Event Log (Event 4663), confirmed the real timeline. The leftover .tmp file from the timestomping tool was the clincher.
debriefing.furtherReading: NTFS MFT structure, Sleuth Kit istat, Windows Event Log 4663/4664, Metasploit post/windows/manage/timestomp

postQuiz.question: Which NTFS attribute is most resistant to timestomping tools and why?
options: $DATA, because it stores the actual file content
$FILE_NAME, because it is updated by the NTFS kernel driver rather than user-space APIs
$STANDARD_INFORMATION, because it requires admin privileges to modify
$OBJECT_ID, because it is write-protected by default
postQuiz.explanation: $FILE_NAME timestamps are maintained directly by the NTFS driver and cannot be changed through standard Windows API calls. This makes them a reliable forensic reference point even after timestomping.

postQuiz.question: What is a reliable indicator that timestomping has occurred?
options: The file size is larger than expected
The file extension does not match its magic bytes
All four $SI timestamps are identical down to the second
The file has no owner assigned
postQuiz.explanation: When all four $SI timestamps (Created, Modified, Accessed, MFT Changed) are precisely the same, it strongly suggests they were set programmatically in a single operation — the hallmark of a timestomping tool.
